lesson.title: The Deliberate Art of Changing a Mind: Persuasion
lesson.summary: Persuasion is the intentional use of communication, whether spoken, written, or visual, to change another person's attitudes or behavior, and psychologists have spent decades studying which features of a message, its source, and its audience make persuasion more or less effective.
lesson.body:
Persuasion is best understood as one specific, deliberate application of the broader social influence processes covered in the previous section. Where social influence theory describes the general mechanisms by which people change because of others, persuasion narrows the focus to cases where someone is intentionally trying to produce that change through a message, whether it is an advertisement, a political speech, a piece of health advice, or a friend's argument during a disagreement. Because persuasion is often aimed at genuine, lasting attitude change rather than mere momentary compliance, the most effective persuasive efforts tend to work through something closer to Kelman's internalization process rather than simple compliance.

Much of the foundational research on persuasion comes from a program led by Carl Hovland and colleagues at Yale University in the 1950s, often referred to as the Yale attitude change approach. This research organized the study of persuasion around a simple but useful structure: who says it, what is said, to whom, and through what channel. Source factors include a communicator's perceived credibility, which itself breaks down into expertise, how knowledgeable the source seems, and trustworthiness, how honest or unbiased the source seems, since a message can be strong on one dimension and weak on the other. Message factors include things like whether an argument presents only one side of an issue or acknowledges the other side as well, and whether the message relies on logical argument, emotional appeal, or fear. Audience factors include the listener's existing attitudes, self esteem, and general willingness to think carefully about the topic at hand, all of which affect how open a given person is to being moved by any particular message.

One notable, if somewhat debated, finding from this tradition is what researchers called the sleeper effect, the observation in some studies that a persuasive message from a low credibility source can, over time, become more influential rather than less, apparently because people tend to forget the source of a message more quickly than they forget its content. This finding has not always replicated cleanly across studies, and psychologists continue to debate exactly when and why it appears, so it is best treated as an interesting but not fully settled pattern rather than a hard and fast rule.

Understanding these building blocks of persuasion, source, message, and audience, raises a deeper question that the Hovland approach did not fully answer on its own: why do the same message and the same source sometimes produce deep, lasting attitude change, and other times produce only a shallow, temporary shift? Answering that question is the job of the next concept, the Elaboration Likelihood Model.
